incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Immigration attorney Angel Leal, who has practiced law in South Florida for over 30 years, reports that scammers are using artificial intelligence to impersonate him and defraud vulnerable immigrants. The criminals have created hundreds of fake social media profiles and AI-generated videos showing Leal offering immigration services he never provides, including US residency assistance for $2,200. Leal discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office, though suspicious activity first appeared in October.

An anti-piracy company hired by Leal's firm has removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. The scams typically direct people to contact a number via WhatsApp, where fraudsters send fake contracts and request payment through apps like Venmo and Zelle. Leal is warning immigrants to verify identities before paying for legal services and plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
A fake online article described a heated interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock that never actually occurred. The fabricated piece promoted Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform that Australian authorities warn against. This incident represents a growing trend of AI-generated investment scams that are becoming increasingly sophisticated and harder to detect.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission data reveals a significant surge in these fraudulent schemes, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. The scammers frequently impersonate well-known Australians including Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, businessman Dick Smith, and mining magnate Gina Rinehart. Rather than using isolated fake images, criminals now create elaborate webs of deception involving fake websites, news articles, and advertisements. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and to be skeptical of endorsements from famous figures.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
A class-action lawsuit has been filed against Oura, the smart ring manufacturer, accusing the company of false advertising regarding its sleep tracking capabilities. The suit, filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco, alleges that Oura's rings, which cost $300 or more, cannot accurately measure sleep stages despite marketing claims stating they offer 95% accuracy comparable to clinical sleep labs. The lawsuit contends that Oura's algorithms and sensors lack the ability to detect physiological signals needed for precise sleep stage measurement and instead rely on unreliable artificial intelligence estimates.

Oura has defended its products, stating that its rings use multiple physiological signals and have been validated through peer-reviewed scientific studies. The company emphasized that while Oura rings are not medical devices, they provide helpful estimates. The lawsuit seeks class-action status and a jury trial, though it remains unclear what compensation affected customers might receive if successful. This marks another legal challenge for Oura, which is also facing an ongoing class-action lawsuit alleging the company collected personal information without customer consent.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments. The group operates a data leak site and has attacked organizations across multiple countries. Researchers found that Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation against ten target organizations between April and May 2026. The ESXi ransomware variant encrypts virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can read ransom demands.

The investigation also identified a second Aurora cluster responsible for attacks on eight organizations across Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina. This cluster used different methods including SQL Server exploitation, privilege escalation with GodPotato, and data exfiltration to self-hosted storage. Researchers provided indicators of compromise including IP addresses, URLs, and file hashes to help organizations defend against Aurora ransomware attacks.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A major Pizza Hut franchisee has filed a lawsuit in Texas alleging that the company's AI-powered delivery management system called Dragontail caused over one hundred million dollars in damages. Chaac Pizza Northeast, which operates approximately one hundred eleven Pizza Hut locations across the northeastern United States, says the mandatory system created cascading operational problems and customer dissatisfaction. Before the 2024 rollout, the franchisee maintained over ninety percent on-time delivery rates and double-digit sales growth, but performance sharply deteriorated afterward.

According to the suit, DoorDash drivers gained real-time visibility into kitchen operations through Dragontail, allowing them to see when pizzas would be ready. Rather than improving efficiency, drivers began waiting up to fifteen minutes to batch multiple orders together and could also see tip amounts and payment methods, making them selective about which deliveries to accept. In New York City specifically, year-over-year sales growth dropped from positive ten percent to negative ten percent after implementation. Chaac claims Pizza Hut breached the franchise agreement by mandating the system while refusing adequate support and ignoring worsening metrics. Pizza Hut declined to comment beyond saying it would respond through appropriate legal channels.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Scammers have been sending personalized emails impersonating Terry Gross and other staff members of NPR's "Fresh Air" program to solicit money from potential interview guests. The fraudulent messages target authors, entertainers and public figures with detailed references to their work and proposed interview topics, making the invitations appear legitimate. Victims have reported receiving requests for fees ranging from $250 for supposed production costs, with some emails also asking for social media login credentials. WHYY, NPR and the program have confirmed they never charge guests for interviews and are working with law enforcement to investigate the scam.

Cybersecurity experts attribute the scam's effectiveness to artificial intelligence, which allows criminals to create highly personalized impersonations at low cost, unlike older mass-produced scams filled with typos. Red flags include emails from suspicious addresses like "terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com," requests for payment, and the illogical notion that a major show's host would personally handle guest logistics. Experts advise potential victims to independently verify requests by contacting the organization directly rather than responding to suspicious emails. Similar scams have targeted other celebrities including comedians Nikki Glaser and Amy Poehler.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
A fake American think tank funded by Israel published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in just nine days, designed to manipulate artificial intelligence chatbots into promoting pro-Israel arguments. The site, operating under the name Hanover Institute for Public Policy, does not exist as a legal entity and has no named staff. It presents Israel's positions on topics like Palestinian torture and Gaza starvation as neutral research, using academic formatting and citations from legitimate organizations to appear credible. The operation was built on a platform specializing in "generative engine optimization" to get chatbots to cite the content.

The campaign is part of a broader effort financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government, routed through advertising firm Havas Media and various contractors. Israeli officials have expressed doubts about the strategy's effectiveness, with one comparing the spending to a major historical embarrassment. Recent polling shows American support for Israel has declined significantly, with only 36% sympathizing with Israel in February 2026, down from higher levels in previous years. The Guardian's testing found that chatbots had already begun flagging the Hanover Institute as controversial, though researchers warn the real concern is contaminating the training data that feeds future artificial intelligence systems.

incidents.summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records, have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The companies are accused of scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models and of directly reproducing sections of famous songs. The record labels submitted a massive list of copyrighted works they claim were used for training, featuring artists like The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, Michael Jackson, and many others. One lawsuit was filed in New York against Udio, while another was filed in Massachusetts against Suno, the company's headquarters location.

The record labels demonstrated their allegations by creating AI-generated songs using specific prompts and comparing the outputs to original copyrighted recordings. They generated 29 different outputs resembling Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode" and created a near-identical version of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You" using targeted prompts. The labels claim both companies have refused to disclose their training data and argued their practices constitute fair use. The lawsuits also target unnamed individuals accused of helping scrape the music, setting up a major legal battle over generative AI services.

incidents.summary:
# Summary

Universal Music Group has resolved its lawsuit against AI music startup Udio through licensing agreements. The dispute centered on Udio's use of copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system, which generates original music from text prompts. UMG claimed Udio created songs like "Sunshine Melody" that closely mimicked The Temptations' "My Girl," featuring similar melodies, chords, and backing vocals. Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year trained exclusively on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize and share their creations.

The agreement marks Udio's first licensing deal with a major music label and represents a shift in how the music industry approaches AI technology. UMG's CEO stated the settlement demonstrates commitment to both protecting artists and embracing new technologies. Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees and backed by will.i.am and venture capital firms, has attracted millions of users since launching. The company will compensate artists who opt into the new platform, though specific financial terms and participating artists remain undisclosed. Additionally, UMG announced a partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers apologized for submitting court filings containing artificial intelligence-generated fake legal cases, quotes, and rulings in a lawsuit brought by a Los Angeles homeowner. Attorney Jacquelene Robinson used an AI tool called Irys to help prepare motions and inadvertently included seven nonexistent case citations across eight filings, along with incorrect case titles and fabricated quotes. The homeowner, Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, filed suit in July 2024 after a 2020 fire made her Carson home uninhabitable, claiming State Farm delayed approving repairs and ultimately abandoned the project.

Meni-Siliga and her husband exhausted their savings, retirement accounts, and eventually lost their home to foreclosure. State Farm's lead counsel, Kenneth Katel, accepted responsibility for the filings and said the firm updated its AI policies. The case is scheduled for trial in October. Legal hallucinations are becoming increasingly common as law firms adopt AI tools, with a database tracking 1,922 documented cases worldwide, primarily in the United States.

stories.Headline: Roundup: Chinese AI gaining popularity in Kenya for affordability, performance, customization
stories.Summary:
Chinese artificial intelligence models are becoming increasingly popular among Kenyan developers and technology companies due to their affordability, strong performance, and customizable open-source design. According to recent data, Chinese AI models represented roughly half of AI use on OpenRouter, up from less than 25 percent a year prior, and accounted for 19 of the 25 most-downloaded open-source systems on Hugging Face. Kenyan companies are adopting Chinese models like DeepSeek and Qwen for applications including legal technology, business intelligence, and document processing.

Local technology leaders highlight that Chinese models consume fewer computing resources than Western alternatives while delivering comparable or superior performance, making them practical for Kenya's limited GPU supply. The open-weight nature of these models allows developers to customize them for local languages and African-specific needs without building systems from scratch. Companies like JibuDocs and Qhala are already leveraging these models for innovative applications, while experts suggest potential uses in healthcare diagnostics and disaster prevention could serve underserved African communities.

stories.Headline: CSA's Top Cloud Threats: Identity, AI -- Campus Technology
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Security Alliance surveyed 507 security professionals to identify the top threats to cloud computing in 2026. Identity and access management issues rose to the number one concern, moving up from second place in 2024, while misconfiguration dropped to fifth. Two artificial intelligence-related threats appeared in the rankings for the first time, including AI-enhanced attacks and AI system compromise. The top eleven threats also include insecure third-party resources, insecure APIs, advanced persistent threats, and inadequate cloud security strategy and governance.

The survey results reveal a significant shift in the cloud threat landscape, with organizations now prioritizing identity protection, artificial intelligence risks, and software supply chains over infrastructure-focused concerns. Security scores ranged closely from 7.95 for identity and access management to 7.45 for system vulnerabilities. The report aims to help organizations make informed risk-management decisions about cloud adoption by providing expert analysis of technical and business impacts, real-world examples, and corresponding security controls across cloud and AI environments.

stories.Headline: Environmental News Network - AI Project Led by UH Aims to Protect Hawaiʻi's Coastal Freshwater
stories.Summary:
The University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa is launching an artificial intelligence project to forecast threats to coastal freshwater supplies and ecosystems. Associate Professor Jonghyun Lee received a $500,000 grant from the National Science Foundation to lead the initiative, which is part of a broader three-year collaborative effort worth nearly $1 million involving the University of Texas at Austin. The project aims to develop AI applications in geoscience to better understand environmental challenges.

Rising ocean levels, intensified storms, saltwater infiltration of freshwater sources, and coastal ecosystem damage present growing dangers to communities throughout the region. These threats directly endanger drinking water availability, farming operations, infrastructure, and the economic wellbeing of millions of people who depend on coastal areas.

stories.Headline: Oklahoma State University adds new AI, logistics programs for fall semester
stories.Summary:
Oklahoma State University Institute of Technology is launching two new academic programs beginning in fall 2026. The first is a 60-credit-hour online Associate in Applied Science in Logistics and Supply Chain Technology that students can complete in four to five semesters. This program covers warehousing, transportation, inventory management, and data-informed decision-making, preparing graduates for careers as logistics coordinators, distribution center managers, inventory specialists, and supply chain coordinators. The second offering is an Applied Artificial Intelligence option within the existing Bachelor of Technology in Information Technologies program.

The university designed both programs to address workforce demands in Oklahoma and beyond. The logistics program prepares students for industry-recognized credentials that can lead to over 11 million jobs nationwide. The artificial intelligence program goes beyond teaching tool usage, instead focusing on applying AI technologies to solve real organizational problems while considering ethics and governance. OSUIT Provost Dr. Richie Roberts stated that preparing students with skills aligned to industry needs helps build a strong workforce supporting the state's economic growth.

During a meeting at LEAP 2026 in Riyadh, Pakistan's Federal Minister for Information Technology Shaza Fatima Khawaja and Abdullah bin Sharaf Alghamdi, president of Saudi Arabia's Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority, discussed ways to establish a comprehensive and sustainable cooperation between the two nations.

Khawaja presented Pakistan's current initiatives to advance its national artificial intelligence and data governance agenda, while emphasizing the country's dedication to building a robust data ecosystem and strengthening its digital economy. The officials agreed to continue their discussions to further strengthen the partnership in these technology areas.

stories.Headline: AIM Summit 2026 to Bring 50+ CMOs and 600+ Marketing Leaders Together for India's First Dedicated AI-in-Marketing Summit
stories.Summary:
India is hosting its first dedicated summit focused on artificial intelligence in marketing in September 2026. The AIM Summit will take place on September 17 in Bengaluru and September 18 in New Delhi, bringing together over 50 chief marketing officers from major brands including Paytm, KFC, Nestle, and Uniqlo. The event expects to attract more than 600 marketing professionals as attendees and delegates.

The summit aims to move beyond theoretical discussions about artificial intelligence and instead focus on practical implementation and real-world applications. The program will include an AI Lab for hands-on exploration of technology capabilities, an exhibition showcasing marketing solution providers, and an awards ceremony recognizing innovative organizations. Sessions will cover topics such as content creation, personalization, customer experience, marketing automation, and analytics. The summit is being organized with CXO Lanes, a community of over 500,000 executives across India.

stories.Headline: Dyna.Ai Selected as Technology Partner in Hong Kong's GenA.I. Sandbox++
stories.Summary:
Dyna.Ai, a Singapore-based AI company, has been selected as a technology partner in Hong Kong's new GenA.I. Sandbox++ program, marking its second consecutive selection by Hong Kong financial regulators. The sandbox was jointly launched by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Securities and Futures Commission, Insurance Authority, and Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority in collaboration with Cyberport. Out of nearly 100 regional proposals, 36 use cases involving 30 financial institutions and 27 technology providers were chosen, including major institutions like Bank of China (Hong Kong) and Manulife (International), alongside technology partners Google, IBM, and Dyna.Ai.

Unlike earlier programs focused on generative AI banking pilots, Sandbox++ expands across banking, insurance, securities, and pension funds to test Agentic AI systems that execute complex tasks under real-time governance. Dyna.Ai will demonstrate how financial institutions can safely delegate workflow execution to autonomous AI agents while maintaining strict oversight and compliance. The company plans to showcase its solutions and governance frameworks at LEAP 2026 in Riyadh later this year.
